newsitem.title: USA: Apple aims to expand Newton platform.
newsitem.headline: Apple aims to expand Newton platform.

text.p: Executives of Apple Computer Inc's Newton Systems Group said the group plans to develop both value-added resellers for its personal digital assistants and to encourage entirely new devices based on its designs.
"We have a strategy where we see this marketplace being very, very diverse," Tony Lee, senior mananger of Information Appliance Licensing at Apple, said in an interview.

Debbie Carlton, director of marketing in the Newton Group, said that based on industry and internal data the market for personal digital assistants (PDAs) is expected to hit some $3 billion in revenues and unit sales of 5.4 million by 1999.
This implies a compound annual growth rate of some 36 percent this year alone, well above the current growth rate for personal computers, she told the 1996 Newton Technology Conference.

In a series of presentations on Apple's strategy, group executives acknowledged products to be unveiled later this month based on Microsoft Corp's new Windows CE system were likely to put pressure on Apple's Newton platform.
Carlton said that out of the systems competing with Newton, the new Windows CE was likely to gain "90 percent of the space."
"I'm sure it's going to be a success because of all the noise that Microsoft will make," she said.

Newton executives and managers said, however, they also expected most of these devices to be more narrowly focussed on desktop connectivity and personal information management, a different approach from the Newton's full solutions for specific markets.

Sandy Benett, vice president of the Newton Systems Group, told Reuters following a presentation to several hundred developers that the group's strategy had evolved since the Newton's heavily hyped launch three years ago.
"I certainly would say we have changed our emphasis. We're not trying to be everything to everybody, we're not what John Sculley said it was three and a half years ago," Benett said.
He was refering to the former Apple chief executive's high promises for Newton that fell far short of Sculley's projections and were a major factor in his subsequent abrupt departure.

Now, Benett said, Apple has three years of market experience and has been developing the platform for more than five years, with five generations of hardware and three generations of software developed over that time.

"The fact other people are getting into the market only adds credence to our effort," he told the presentation. "We're now targeted towards certain markets, certain vertical applications, certain horizontal applications."

For example, Apple shared details of its MessagePad 2000 and its eMate 300 educational system unveiled last week. Both machines are in production and are due to ship at under $1000 and under $800, respectively, in the first quarter of 1997.

The MessagePad 2000 uses the StrongARM processor designed by Advanced RISC Machines LTD and built by Digital Equipment Corp. They use nickel metal hydride batteries that run for more than 20 hours on a one-hour charge or for up to six weeks of use.

Tony Lee said Newton was working to refresh the market for other companies to develop machines on the Newton platform, both by manufacturing for third parties that add custom casings and applications and by publishing a reference platform design, to be issued by the end of calendar 1997.

Apple described two wireless devices marketed by Digital Ocean offering handheld wireless capabilities based on the Newton MessagePad 130, and a product Schlumberger is developing for France's healthcare market based on the 2000.

"People like Schlumberger, they understand the market, they looked at all the technologies and they decided to go with a derivative of the MessagePad 2000," he said. "We think there are multiple opportunities for people to do that."

The Newton executives said they expect multiple form factors at a wide variety of price points with different degrees of modularity, localization and software that recognises handwriting or basic voice commands.
"Think forward into the future as to your applications," Lee urged the developers.
